item.title: All-Microwave Multiqubit Gates
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Single-step (n+m) multiqubit gates implemented on transmon networks via cross-resonance drives without tunable couplers. Three-qubit gates reach simulated fidelities >99.9% in 60 ns.

Grade 0.471 · 3.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “transmon and fluxonium coherence, single- and two-qubit gate fidelity” · Guanqi Wang, Yao Song, Peng-Bo Li, Xiu-Hao Deng

Figure

Gate infidelity versus optimization iteration and target Pauli operation fidelity across three-qubit gates and larger multi-target configurations, showing convergence below 10−3.

Asks

How can single-step multiqubit gates with n control and m target transmons be implemented with all-microwave control without tunable couplers?

But

Numerical simulation only. Dispersive regime with shared or near-degenerate target frequencies and suppressed parasitic terms such as ZXX.

Tools

cross-resonance microwave drives · quad frame rotation · block diagonalization · gradient-based pulse optimization

Abstract

Implementing high-fidelity multiqubit gates is critical for reducing circuit depth in near-term quantum processors and fault-tolerant architectures. However, realizing multiqubit interactions and entanglement remains a critical challenge that limits the implementation of multiqubit gates. Here we propose an all-microwave scheme to realize single-step multiqubit gates incorporating n control and m target qubits, tailored for frequency-tunable superconducting transmon networks. By leveraging cross-resonance (CR) drives, this approach induces effective two-body ZX interactions that are significantly stronger than those achieved in conventional resonant regimes, circumventing the need for tunable couplers. The system's effective Hamiltonian is analytically derived using both quad frame rotation and rigorous block diagonalization. These combined theoretical methods facilitate the identification of optimal parameter regimes that simultaneously enhance desired target couplings and suppress parasitic higher-order terms, such as ZXX interactions. Through numerical simulations and gradient-based pulse-shape optimization, we demonstrate three-qubit gates achieving fidelities exceeding 99.9% within a 60 ns gate duration. Furthermore, we evaluate the fundamental scalability of this framework by extending the optimization to a five-qubit CXXXX architecture, confirming the physical viability of the multi-target driving scheme. Because these multiqubit operations naturally emulate stabilizer measurements, this architecture provides a hardware-efficient strategy for reducing the circuit depth of stabilizer-type operations by replacing sequential two-qubit gate decompositions with single-step multiqubit gates.

item.title: Reservoir- and Measurement-free Microwave Initialization of Semiconductor Spin Qubits
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Fixed-sequence microwave and baseband initialization prepares singlet-associated charge state with 99.4% median probability without electron reservoirs or measurement feedback. Sequence uses ~12 μs of microwave bursts and mixing dwells in Si/SiGe quantum dots.

Grade 0.450 · 2.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Silicon quantum electronics” · Leon C. Camenzind, Ik Kyeong Jin, Akito Noiri, Kenta Takeda, Takashi Nakajima, Takashi Kobayashi, Seigo Tarucha

Figure

Measured initialization probability as a function of cycle repetitions for different initial spin states, showing convergence to >99% singlet state via repeated microwave-driven triplet transfer and mixing dwells.

Asks

Can semiconductor spin-qubit pairs be initialized rapidly using only fixed microwave and baseband pulses, without local reservoir exchange or active measurement-based feedback?

But

Single-cycle transfer bounded by 0.5 dark-state limit; total time excludes fixed baseband transport overheads and readout verification.

Tools

three-qubit Si/SiGe device · electric-dipole spin resonance · radio-frequency reflectometry · Pauli spin blockade

Abstract

Scalable quantum processors require repeated qubit initialization throughout large arrays. In semiconductor spin qubits, fast initialization commonly relies on local reservoir access or measurement-based feedback, requiring dedicated infrastructure that becomes increasingly difficult to distribute as processors scale. Here, we demonstrate reservoir- and measurement-free initialization of a silicon spin-qubit pair in an industrially fabricated Si/SiGe quantum-dot device using a fixed sequence of microwave and baseband pulses. Odd spin-parity states relax to the singlet charge state, whereas blocked even spin-parity states are microwave-driven through the triplet manifold and subsequently converted to the singlet by singlet-triplet mixing and charge hybridization. Repeated cycles produce the singlet-associated charge outcome with a median probability of 99.4% across the sampled preparation states, while exchange spectroscopy independently verifies mapping to the target |↑↓⟩ operational state. Microwave spectroscopy and time-domain measurements identify the dark-state-limited single-cycle transfer and the subsequent blockade-lifting dynamics that set the initialization time scale. The demonstrated pumping sequence uses approximately 12 μs of microwave bursts and mixing dwells, while we project sub-microsecond initialization under improved device conditions. These results establish fixed-sequence microwave initialization as a scalable control primitive for semiconductor spin-qubit processors, based on singlet-triplet physics that can be adapted to platforms with suitable Pauli-blockade transitions.

item.title: Qantum Well Resonant Tunneling Diode Probe of Correlated States in Twisted Bilayer MoS₂
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Near-AB-stacked ≈57∘ tMoS2 exhibits a robust correlated insulating state at ν=1 across all measured displacement fields, and an emergent fractional insulating state at ν=3/4 for D<−75 mV/nm that disappears above 12 K.

Grade 0.416 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Chengjie Zhou, Jin-Xin Hu, Sihong Xu, Zijing Jin, Hui Li, Kam Tuen Law, Jiannong Wang

Figure

Differential conductance dI/dVProbe versus filling factor ν and vertical displacement field D at 2 K. Dips mark the continuous insulating state at ν=1 and the emergent fractional state at ν=3/4 below −75 mV/nm.

Asks

Can correlated electronic states in the electron-doped flat bands of near-AB-stacked twisted bilayer MoS2 be probed locally with dual-gate field control?

But

Tested on two devices (twist angles ≈57∘ and ≈56.5∘) at temperatures from 1.7 K to 100 K and magnetic fields up to 9 T.

Tools

quantum well resonant tunneling diode (QWRTD) · vertical tunneling differential conductance (dI/dV_Probe) · dual-gate electrostatics · twisted bilayer MoS₂

Abstract

Moiré superlattices formed in transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) offer a versatile platform for exploring emergent quantum phases arising from strong electronic correlations. In this work, we develop a new experimental platform, the quantum well resonant tunneling diode (QWRTD), to probe the electronic landscape of ≈57^∘ twisted bilayer MoS₂ (tMoS₂). By measuring the differential conductance (dI/dV_Probe) as a function of filling factor ν and displacement field D, we observe a robust integer correlated insulating state at ν= 1 that persists across the measured displacement field range. Furthermore, we identify a displacement-field-induced fractional insulating state at ν= 3/4 for D < -75~mV/nm. Temperature- and magnetic-field-dependent measurements characterize this ν= 3/4 state as a potential generalized Wigner crystal. These correlated states are also observed in another device with a similar twist angle (≈56.5^∘). Our results provide direct evidence of correlated states in near-AB-stacked tMoS₂ and establish QWRTD as a powerful experimental tool for investigating strong correlations and topology in van der Waals heterostructures.

item.title: Quantum double lock-in detection via sequential orthogonal quantum mixing
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Single-interferometer quantum double lock-in detection extracts amplitude A, frequency ω, and initial phase β of an oscillating signal, achieving Heisenberg-limited precisions ΔA,Δω,Δβ∝1/N with an N-particle GHZ probe and interaction-based readout.

Grade 0.401 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “circuit QED dispersive readout and Purcell-limited measurement” · Min Zhuang, Sijie Chen, Jiahao Huang, Chaohong Lee

Figure

Log-log scaling of measurement precisions ΔA, Δω, and Δβ versus particle number N, showing 1/N standard quantum limit for spin-coherent states and 1/N Heisenberg scaling for GHZ states.

Asks

Can quantum double lock-in detection extract full amplitude, frequency, and phase information from an unknown oscillating signal using a single quantum interferometry while achieving Heisenberg-limited precision?

Before

Conventional quantum double lock-in detection requires two separate quantum interferometers, each requiring state preparation and readout (was ∝1/N scaling without entanglement).

But

Theoretical derivation assuming instantaneous π pulses and noiseless state initialization. Gaussian detection noise σ=0.5N degrades scaling to between SQL and Heisenberg limit.

Tools

Periodic dynamical decoupling (PDD) sequences · Carr-Purcell (CP) sequences · Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states · Fast Fourier transform (FFT) / Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR) analysis

Abstract

High-precision measurement of oscillating signal is a ubiquitous issue in fundamental science and a critical task in practical technologies. In quantum metrology, quantum lock-in detection provide an efficient method for measuring such signal. In general, when the initial phase of the oscillating signal is unknown,quantum double lock-in detection can effectively extract complete information about the signal's amplitude, frequency, and initial phase. Conventional quantum double lock-in detection requires two individual quantum interferometry, each of which must undergo state preparation and readout. However, the time for state preparation and readout need not be negligible in practical experiments. In particular, the time for state preparation is longer than the time for sensing. To save experimental resources, it is challenging to achieve quantum double lock-in detection just via a single quantum interferometry while still extracting complete information about the signal's amplitude, frequency, and initial phase. Here, we present a general protocol for achieving a quantum double lock-in detection just via a single quantum interferometry under a sequential orthogonal periodic multipulse sequences. In particular, if the input state is a Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state and two interaction-based operations are applied during interferometry, the measurement precisions for frequency, amplitude, and initial phase can both approach the Heisenberg limit. Our study paves a new way for measuring oscillating signals with a single quantum interferometry, and provides a feasible method for achieving Heisenberg-limited detection of alternating signals.

item.title: Multi-Branch Transport in a Back-gated WS₂ Transistor at Deep-Cryogenic Temperature
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Back-gated multilayer WS2 transistor operates down to 20 mK with an on/off current ratio >105 and reproducible multi-stage turn-on shoulders described by parallel conduction branches.

Grade 0.397 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “materials-limited loss: two-level systems, interfaces, valley splitting” · Megan Powell, Vilas Patil, Hazel Neill, Stephen O'Sullivan, Paul K. Hurley, Lida Ansari, Farzan Gity, Alessandro Rossi

Figure

Drain current IDS plotted against back-gate voltage VGS from 20 mK to 25 K at VDS=0.5 V, showing multi-stage turn-on and extracted on/off current ratios exceeding 105 across the full temperature range.

Asks

How do the electrical transport and turn-on characteristics of a back-gated multilayer WS2 field-effect transistor evolve at deep-cryogenic temperatures down to the millikelvin regime?

Before

was on/off ratio ≈104 at 77 K for WSe2 devices (reference 16)

But

Single back-gated device on Si/SiO2 with Ni/Au contacts; transport influenced by contact barriers, trap states, and electrostatic disorder.

Tools

mechanically exfoliated multilayer WS₂ flake (∼90~nm) · dilution refrigerator (20~mK ≤T ≤25~K) · multi-branch Lambert-W conduction model · density functional theory (DFT)

Abstract

Two-dimensional materials are promising candidates for electronic applications beyond the operating limits of conventional semiconductor technologies. Within this class, transition-metal dichalcogenides offer attractive properties for field-effect transistor operation, with tungsten disulphide (WS₂) emerging as a particularly promising material for operation at cryogenic temperatures. Here, we investigate the electrical performance of a back-gated multilayer WS₂ transistor at deep cryogenic temperature, down to 20 mK. The device remains strongly gate-tunable throughout the cryogenic regime, with an effective on/off current ratio exceeding 10⁵. Most notably, the low-temperature turn-on characteristics exhibit reproducible shoulder-like features, which we describe using a phenomenological model comprising multiple effective conduction branches operating in parallel.

item.title: Optical observation of interlayer spin correlation
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Two-magnon Raman scattering measures dynamical interlayer spin correlations ⟨(𝐒ˆA⋅𝐒ˆB)(t)(𝐒ˆA⋅𝐒ˆB)(0)⟩, observing two-magnon features at 46 meV and 82 meV in CrSBr that vanish above TC∼150 K and collapse under out-of-plane field as (1−(B/Bsat)2)2. Exciton-resonant excitation at 908 nm enhances two-magnon intensity roughly tenfold.

Grade 0.394 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Akiyoshi Park, Pranshoo Upadhyay, Andrey Grankin, Emil Viñas Boström, Mahdi Ghafariasl, Hassan Alnatah, Masoud Mohammadi-Arzanagh, Gautam Nambiar, Beini Gao, Alireza Alvandi, Sakthi Rajmano Madhan Kumar, Ghadah Alshalan, Isaac Sherwood, Mahmoud Jalali Mehrabad, You Zhou, Arun Ramanathan, Xavier Roy, Angel Rubio, Mohammad Hafezi

Figure

Measured (top) and calculated (bottom) Raman spectrum of CrSBr versus Raman shift. Shows three sharp low-frequency Ag phonon peaks and a broad two-magnon continuum spanning ∼45 to 100 meV with band edge at 46 meV and peak at 82 meV.

Asks

Can interlayer spin–spin correlations in layered van der Waals antiferromagnets be directly probed by optical spectroscopy?

But

Measured on bulk CrSBr at T=3.5 K; two-magnon channel vanishes in field-induced ferromagnetic state above Bsat≈2.1 T.

Tools

Two-magnon Raman spectroscopy · Fleury–Loudon light–matter interaction modeling · CrSBr van der Waals antiferromagnet · Exciton resonance enhancement

Abstract

Spin correlations govern numerous collective behaviors of quantum materials, underpinning exotic phenomena such as unconventional superconductivity and topological magnetism. In layered materials, the interlayer spin correlation is important because it characterizes the magnetic ground state and determines spin transport across the interface. Yet interlayer spin correlations have remained hard to measure directly, leaving one of the most basic quantities of two-dimensional magnetism out of experimental reach. Here we provide the first direct optical probe of interlayer spin correlations, using two-magnon Raman scattering in the van der Waals antiferromagnet (AFM) CrSBr, in remarkable agreement with a microscopic spin-wave model without any fitting parameter. Moreover, the two-magnon channel switches on only in the AFM state and vanishes when a magnetic field takes the crystal to a ferromagnetic state. We furthermore establish an exciton-mediated variant of the technique, where tuning the laser near the exciton resonance enhances the signal roughly tenfold due to the exciton's large oscillator strength. Magnon-pair Raman spectroscopy thus opens a direct optical window into interlayer spin correlations in van der Waals magnets, extendable to twisted bilayers and proximity-coupled heterostructures.

Exciton-resonant excitation at 908 nm enhances two-magnon intensity roughly tenfold.

item.arxave:tools: Two-magnon Raman spectroscopy · Fleury–Loudon light–matter interaction modeling · CrSBr van der Waals antiferromagnet · Exciton resonance enhancement
item.arxave:abstract: Spin correlations govern numerous collective behaviors of quantum materials, underpinning exotic phenomena such as unconventional superconductivity and topological magnetism. In layered materials, the interlayer spin correlation is important because it characterizes the magnetic ground state and determines spin transport across the interface. Yet interlayer spin correlations have remained hard to measure directly, leaving one of the most basic quantities of two-dimensional magnetism out of experimental reach. Here we provide the first direct optical probe of interlayer spin correlations, using two-magnon Raman scattering in the van der Waals antiferromagnet (AFM) CrSBr, in remarkable agreement with a microscopic spin-wave model without any fitting parameter. Moreover, the two-magnon channel switches on only in the AFM state and vanishes when a magnetic field takes the crystal to a ferromagnetic state. We furthermore establish an exciton-mediated variant of the technique, where tuning the laser near the exciton resonance enhances the signal roughly tenfold due to the exciton's large oscillator strength. Magnon-pair Raman spectroscopy thus opens a direct optical window into interlayer spin correlations in van der Waals magnets, extendable to twisted bilayers and proximity-coupled heterostructures.

item.title: Complex Quantum Dynamics Versus Classical Simulability of Noisy Random Circuits
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Dynamical diagnostics (magic, scrambling, anticoncentration, non-Gaussianity) decouple from classical simulation hardness in noisy quantum circuits. Local depolarising noise damps fourth-order Pauli moments asymptotically twice as fast as second-order moments, causing magic to vanish at depth Θ(N) while efficient classical sampling threshold remains Θ(1) under sparse noise.

Grade 0.393 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play” · Anjali Waghmare, Sergii Strelchuk, Sathyawageeswar Subramanian

Figure

Circuit depth versus depolarising noise parameter (or dephasing parameter). Dashed curves mark dynamical resource boundaries; solid colors mark fastest classical simulation algorithms, showing the dynamical boundary crosscuts classical simulation efficiency regions in both directions.

Asks

In noisy quantum circuits, do dynamical diagnostics such as magic, scrambling, and anticoncentration reliably track classical simulability?

But

Depolarising noise on brickwork Clifford+T and Majorana dephasing on matchgate+SWAP circuits.

Tools

fourth-order Clifford commutant · Pauli-path truncation · Majorana transfer matrix · replica transfer matrix

Abstract

Claims of quantum advantage rest on the classical hardness of simulating quantum circuits. Magic, operator scrambling, anticoncentration, and non-Gaussianity for fermionic circuits are standard diagnostics of complex quantum dynamics. For pure states, some of these have been rigorously connected to classical simulability. Whether these diagnostics reliably track the limits of efficient classical simulation under noise remains unclear. Here, we show that in noisy Clifford+T and nearest-neighbour matchgate+SWAP circuits, dynamical diagnostics and classical simulability can separate in both directions. In particular, the diagnostics can remain nontrivial after classical simulation becomes efficient, or become trivial before known efficient classical algorithms apply. We trace this mismatch to the different statistical properties they probe: magic and scrambling depend on fourth-order statistics of the Pauli spectrum, whereas the simulation algorithms depend primarily on second-order moments, which local noise suppresses at different rates. Thus, dynamical diagnostics measured on a noisy quantum device do not by themselves constitute evidence for classical hardness.

item.title: CSS codes for Quantum Metrology with Discrete-time Error Correction
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Discrete-time CSS quantum error correction preserves Heisenberg-like temporal scaling δω∝T−1 against perpendicular noise within an interrogation window scaling as tp∼1/τ, before crossing over to SQL-like scaling δω∝T−1/2. Single recovery applied solely at interrogation end yields zero metrological advantage.

Grade 0.390 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play” · Ugnė Liaubaitė, Debora Ramacciotti, Robert Raußendorf

Figure

Frequency sensitivity versus total sensing time budget T for Steane and Shor codes across correction intervals τ. Sensitivity scales linearly (T−1) up to optimal interrogation time topt, then transitions to square-root scaling (T−1/2).

Asks

How does finite-frequency discrete error correction with Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes preserve parameter sensitivity and affect the Heisenberg-to-SQL crossover under perpendicular Markovian noise?

But

Instantaneous and ideal recovery operations; initial logical-plus state |+L⟩⊗k without noise optimization; local Z signal Hamiltonian and perpendicular Markovian X noise.

Tools

CSS stabilizer codes (Steane, Shor) · Adjoint Lindblad master equation · Discrete syndrome extraction and recovery map · Classical Fisher information of stabilizer projector

Abstract

The goal of quantum metrology is to estimate an unknown parameter with better-than-classical precision and, ideally, to attain Heisenberg scaling. In realistic settings, however, noise can substantially reduce this advantage and, in many cases, restore standard-quantum-limit-like performance. Preserving the quantum enhancement therefore requires noise-robust strategies, which can be implemented using quantum error correction. In this work, we develop and analyze a quantum-metrology protocol based on Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes. The main result is that, for noise perpendicular to the sensing Hamiltonian, discrete-time error correction preserves Heisenberg-like temporal scaling over a finite interrogation-time window whose duration depends on the correction frequency. It is further shown that recovery applied only after the sensing evolution provides no metrological advantage over the corresponding uncorrected noisy protocol in the setup considered here. An analytical framework is developed for arbitrary CSS codes and applied to the Steane and Shor codes, for which the discrete-time corrected dynamics, the Heisenberg-like-to-SQL-like crossover, and the optimal interrogation time are determined and numerically analysed.
